book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

chapters.relation: Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.

Applies Husserl's phenomenology - noesis (the act of meaning-giving), noema (the meaning arrived at), and the life-world - to Voyager's Doctor and Seven of Nine as they build selves from conscious experience. Reads "Latent Image" (the Doctor's deleted memories of choosing Harry Kim's life over another ensign's) and "Infinite Regress" (Seven's channeling of assimilated personalities) as parallel guilt experiences whose noemata teach each that past choices remain part of identity without governing it. Their forced isolation in "One", the Doctor's unrequited love in "Someone to Watch over Me", and "Body and Soul", where the Doctor savors food and sensation through Seven's body, generate a shared noema: social interaction and embodied experience are what make a life-world, even for photons and drones.

Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.

chapters.file: ch29 - Part IV Gamma Quadrant Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations.md

chapters.relation: Argues through Alfred North Whitehead's philosophy of organism - reality as momentary actual occasions with mental and physical poles, nested societies, and canalization - that Star Trek's advanced beings are not, and could not be, purely incorporeal. Mindless feeders like the dikironium cloud creature and the Drella show bodilessness is not sufficient for advancement, while parasitic Zetars and Ronin show it can be a liability; the Douwd, the Companion, and Amanda Rogers's Q parents voluntarily tether to bodies for love and new experience. The Q's stagnation and civil war ("Death Wish", "The Q and the Grey") illustrate Whitehead's balance of survival against creative advance: what looks like "freedom from physical form" is really "freedom of physical form", since a purely mental entity would be an unsustainable organism.

Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.

Pits Donna Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto against Star Trek's horror of the Borg, reading Locutus/Picard, Hugh, and Seven of Nine as tests of the Federation values of autonomy, individuality, and authenticity against the rival Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation. Picard's "My culture is based on freedom and self-determination" exchange with the Borg, Hugh's discovery of his name and first-person "I", and Seven's tug-of-war with the Borg Queen in "Dark Frontier" dramatize what assimilation threatens. The chapter then defends a Haraway-inspired feminist reboot: women and minorities were long denied autonomy, individuality, and authenticity by prejudice and stereotype (Seven still must look "warp-core hot" in her catsuit), the human/machine and man/woman binaries were always false, and since we already live as cyborgs of apps, implants, and networks, resistance was negligible - the real Borg problem is their violent means, not their values.

Uses Odo as a case study in George Herbert Mead's theory that the self emerges only through social interaction: language begins with significant gestures (Odo's tentacle-slap at Dr. Mora, his talking to the dying baby changeling in "The Begotten"), and specific others like Mora and Kira teach the attitudes that become the generalized other. The Meadian I/me split explains Ezri Dax's nine-selves crisis and Joran's emergence in "Field of Fire", and the failed outfield calls and Sisko's ejection of Rom in "Take Me out to the Holosuite" show characters still learning to take the attitude of the team. Odo's "justice trick" is reread as instinct rather than racial memory, his confession to Kira in "Heart of Stone" shows the name odo'ital ("nothing") redeemed by internalized others, and his choice of the station crew over the Great Link marks a cosmopolitan self.

Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.

Reads the Borg as the embodiment of Heidegger's essence of technology: assimilation as the "challenging" that sets upon nature, species and persons as standing-reserve, drones interchangeable like replaceable parts, and cube ships with no bridge because function outweighs individuality. The Enterprise cannot beat the Borg with more technology - every phaser adaptation buys only moments - because, as with Heidegger's danger, the crew tries to control technology from inside technology; rescue comes only when Guinan persuades Riker to "throw the book away" and shift how the crew relates to the Borg. The warning is extended to us through Zizek on synthetic life and a new servant class and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: our devices already remember, plan, and identify for us, so we are being assimilated by our own creations.

chapters.file: ch36 - Part V Beyond the Galactic Barrier The Future as the Final Frontier.md

chapters.relation: Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.

Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.

Reads "The City on the Edge of Forever" through Romanticism: the Guardian of Forever strands Kirk and Spock without historical reference points - a nihilist moment of pure meaninglessness - and Kirk's Romantic response is to rebuild the narrative of the past even at the cost of letting Edith Keeler die. Hegel's philosophy of history explains the compulsion to record (Spock's anguished "I've missed taping centuries of living history"), why Edith's unwitting world-historical role is to die under a truck rather than lead a pacifist America to Nazi conquest, and Novalis's call to "make the world Romantic" frames Spock's self-rescue as young Selek in "Yesteryear". Kirk, Spock, and McCoy become Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy archetypes - Tragic Hero, Apollonian, Dionysian - converging in the street scene where McCoy lunges to save Edith, Spock waits on logic, and Kirk, seizing McCoy's arms, finds a tragic beauty in her death.

Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few. The lesson of "Tapestry" is amor fati: Picard must embrace the Nausicaan knife fight that nearly killed him, since undoing it makes a safe, unnoticed man - though the authors finally refuse Nietzsche's harsher dictum that the weak should perish, siding with healing over Q's education-by-death.

Argues that despite Roddenberry's strident atheism, Star Trek develops a "humanist theology": godlike beings - Gary Mitchell, Charlie X, Trelane, Q, and Apollo in "Who Mourns for Adonais?" - are demoted to powerful aliens whose demand for worship disqualifies them as gods, echoing the 1960s death-of-God theology in which god-figures are consistently disappointing and the God of traditional theism is symbolically dead. Divinity is relocated into a possible human future requiring compassion above power - Kirk's charge to the dying Mitchell that "a god needs compassion", and Picard's "perhaps there's a residue of humanity in Q after all". The chapter also weighs Trek's anti-posthuman bias ("Dr. Korby was never here", the Borg) against the consensual Decker-V'Ger union in The Motion Picture, and reads Star Trek V's "What does God need with a starship?" as the uneasy remainder of Shatner's religiosity inside Roddenberry's secular vision.

Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.

holes.name: Annette Baier
holes.what: Contemporary feminist moral philosopher whose account of persons as "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood through long dependency, care, and mutual recognition anchors chapter 26's model of human nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central argument that Data, Seven of Nine, and the Doctor become persons through socialization is built directly on Baier's quoted account of personhood, and no existing slug covers it.

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher whose metaphysics of actual occasions, organisms, and societies supplies chapter 30's entire framework for judging advanced life-forms.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is wholly built on Whitehead's philosophy of organism to argue the Q and Organians cannot be purely incorporeal, and the taxonomy has no process-philosophy entry.

holes.name: Philosophy of Organism (process philosophy)
holes.what: Whitehead's view that reality consists of momentary experiential occasions with mental and physical poles organized into nested societies, where survival must balance creative intensity.
holes.why: Chapter 30 applies actual occasions, standing societies, and canalization to Organians, cloud-creatures, and the Q Continuum; nothing in the taxonomy captures process metaphysics.

holes.name: Neera Badhwar
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of friendship whose paper "Why It Is Wrong to Be Always Guided by the Best: Consequentialism and Friendship" argues consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship.
holes.why: Chapter 31's core thesis - that Spock's consequentialism cannot accommodate Kirk's friendship - is Badhwar's argument, quoted extensively, and she is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist science-studies theorist whose 1985 "A Cyborg Manifesto" celebrates the human-machine hybrid as a way out of oppositional dualisms.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is framed entirely by Haraway's "I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess" against the Borg, and she is missing from the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto)
holes.what: Haraway's figure of the human-machine hybrid as ontology and politics, dissolving boundaries between organism and machine and rejecting hierarchical binaries.
holes.why: Chapter 32 defends Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation precisely through the cyborg concept; the generic feminism slug does not carry this specific machinery.

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American social behaviorist whose theory of the socially emergent self (the I and the me, specific and generalized others, significant symbols and play) structures chapter 33.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is a sustained application of Mead's Mind, Self, and Society to Odo, and Mead does not appear in the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Social Self (I and Me)
holes.what: Mead's account of the self as emerging from social interaction: the impulsive I responding to the internalized attitudes (the me) of specific and generalized others, learned through language and play.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explains Odo's personhood through the I/me distinction, gesture-language, and taking the attitude of the team; the generic personal-identity slug does not cover this developmental social theory.

holes.name: Mary Midgley
holes.what: Twentieth-century British moral philosopher known for her critique of moral isolationism in "Trying Out One's New Sword".
holes.why: Chapter 34's resolution of the cogenitor dilemma rests on Midgley's anti-isolationism and her tsujigiri example, and she is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Moral Isolationism (judging other cultures)
holes.what: Midgley's target view that we cannot criticize cultures outside our own; she argues respect requires understanding, which makes informed cross-cultural judgment both possible and necessary.
holes.why: Chapter 34 applies this concept to Trip's judgment of Vissian cogenitor treatment and to Quark's cross-species critique, and no existing slug names the view being attacked.

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Contemporary continental philosopher who extends Heideggerian worries about technology to synthetic life, ungoverned biogenetic research, and a new servant underclass.
holes.why: Chapter 35's concluding move - that the Borg warning has already arrived in synthetic biology and class division - is carried by Žižek's cited work, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Novalis
holes.what: German Romantic poet-philosopher (Friedrich von Hardenberg) who called for making the world Romantic - a qualitative raising of the ordinary to a higher power.
holes.why: Chapter 39 quotes Novalis's "the world must be made Romantic" as the key to Spock's taping of history and his Yesteryear self-rescue, and no Romantic figure exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Romanticism (the world must be made Romantic)
holes.what: The intellectual movement (c. 1770-1850) reacting against Enlightenment rationalization by treating imagination, nature, death, and irony as sources of meaning against nihilism.
holes.why: Chapter 39 explicitly reads "The City on the Edge of Forever" and "Yesteryear" through Romanticism, including the romantic focal point of history and beauty-in-death; the taxonomy has no Romanticism entry.

holes.name: Secular Humanism
holes.what: The worldview centering human values and flourishing without recourse to a transcendent deity, here extended into Roddenberry's "humanist theology" of humanity's divine potential.
holes.why: Chapter 41's title concept is Star Trek's humanist theology - Roddenberry's atheism, the demand-for-worship test, and compassion as the divine attribute - and no taxonomy slug names humanism itself.

holes.name: Secularization (religion and the public sphere)
holes.what: The political and social doctrine that public reason and government should operate independently of religious authority, balancing political democracy against civil liberties including freedom from religion.
holes.why: Chapter 42's moral arguments for a secular society (Picard refusing to be the Mintakans' god, Akorem's D'jarra theocracy) need this concept; democracy-theory alone misses the religion-in-politics dimension.
